etymology: A contraction of the Middle English arayment, “array, that with which one is arrayed,” from Old French areer, “to array, to set in order”; hence clothing, apparel, the garments that cover and adorn the body.
biblical_def: Raiment is the old word for clothing, the apparel with which a man is arrayed and covered. It stands among the first riches of the world: when Abraham’s servant would win Rebekah, he brought forth “jewels of silver, and jewels of gold, and raiment” (Gen 24:53), for garments were treasure, given and inherited and stored up. Yet Scripture bends the word toward the soul. Our Lord forbids anxious care: “Take no thought… for your body, what ye shall put on…. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?” (Mat 6:25). The body is greater than what clothes it, and the God who clothes the lilies will clothe His own. Soft raiment marks the courts of kings (Mat 11:8), but John the Baptist wore camel’s hair in the wilderness, and the kingdom is not of soft clothing but of repentance. The word rises highest in the counsel of Christ to Laodicea: “buy of me… white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear” (Rev 3:18). Here raiment is the imputed righteousness of Christ, the wedding garment without which no man is fit for the marriage supper. Fallen Adam sewed fig leaves and hid; the LORD clothed him with coats of skins, a beast slain in his stead. So the gospel offers a raiment not woven by the wearer but bought of Christ — white, spotless, covering the shame of our nakedness before God.
webster_summary: Clothing, garments, apparel; that with which the body is arrayed and covered.
webster_full: RAIMENT, clothing in general; vestments; garments; apparel.
That with which the body is arrayed and covered from nakedness.
Anciently reckoned among riches, given and inherited as treasure.
In Scripture, the daily provision the LORD promises to His own.
Figuratively, the white raiment of Christ’s righteousness (Rev 3:18).

Mat 6:25

Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?
Mat 11:8
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? behold, they that wear soft clothing are in kings' houses.
Rev 3:18

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for clothing; it recovers the promise that God clothes His own and the greater raiment of Christ’s righteousness.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the anxious care of the age, which loads itself with thought for what it shall put on and forgets that the life is more than raiment. Men who fret over the covering of the body will not lift their eyes to the covering of the soul; they will spend for soft clothing and go naked before God. The lilies neither toil nor spin, yet Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of them — and the God who so clothes the grass of the field will not fail to clothe the children who seek first His kingdom.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that our best raiment is not woven by us. Adam covered his nakedness with fig leaves and was still ashamed; the LORD clothed him with the skins of a slain beast. So the gospel bids us buy of Christ white raiment, that the shame of our nakedness do not appear — a righteousness imputed, not earned, the wedding garment without which the King casts a man into outer darkness. To be clothed with Christ is to be dressed for the marriage supper of the Lamb.
roots_summary: The word means apparel, that with which the body is arrayed and covered.
roots_lines: Raiment — a contraction of Middle English arayment, “array.”
From Old French areer, “to array, to set in order.”
It denotes clothing, garments, the apparel of the body.
Anciently it was counted among riches and treasure (Gen 24:53).
It figures the white raiment of Christ’s righteousness (Rev 3:18).
usage: Take no thought for raiment: the God who clothes the lilies will clothe His own.
Soft raiment fills kings’ houses, but the wilderness preacher wore camel’s hair and preached repentance.
Buy of Christ white raiment, that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear before God.

etymology: From the Old English glæs, “glass,” used in the KJV not for spectacles but for the polished hand-mirror; in Isaiah the plural names the looking-glasses among the finery of the daughters of Zion.
biblical_def: In the KJV a “glass” is not a windowpane nor a drinking vessel but a mirror — anciently a disc of polished metal in which one beheld a dim and imperfect image. Among the twenty-odd ornaments the LORD threatens to strip from the haughty daughters of Zion, Isaiah numbers “the glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails” (Isa 3:23): the hand-mirrors of the vain, the very tools of self-admiration, listed with the bracelets and the changeable suits of apparel as so much finery that judgment will sweep away. The word gathers a doctrine. Paul makes the glass a figure of our present partial knowledge: “now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face” (1Co 13:12) — the polished metal gave only a shadowed likeness, as our knowledge of God is now dim beside the sight of glory. Yet the glass also transforms: “we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory” (2Co 3:18). To gaze upon Christ is to be conformed to Him. And James warns of the man who is a hearer only, “like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass” who straightway forgets what manner of man he was (Jas 1:23). The mirror of the daughters of Zion flatters; the mirror of the Word convicts, and the mirror of Christ’s glory conforms.
webster_summary: A mirror, anciently of polished metal, giving a dim reflected image; in Isaiah, the hand-mirrors among the finery of the daughters of Zion.
webster_full: GLASS, in old usage a mirror, made of polished metal, for beholding the face.
Its image was dim and imperfect beside the clearness of direct sight.
In Isaiah, the plural names the looking-glasses of the vain and haughty (Isa 3:23).
Figuratively, our present partial knowledge, seen “through a glass, darkly” (1Co 13:12).
Also the glass of the Word, wherein a man beholds his true face (Jas 1:23).
scriptures: Isa 3:23
The glasses, and the fine linen, and the hoods, and the vails.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.
Jas 1:23
For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass:
corruption_summary: A word for the mirror, and one the age misreads: the glasses of Zion were tools of self-admiration, and ours has made the looking-glass a throne.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, spoken in the age’s own vocabulary. The glasses of the daughters of Zion were the instruments of vanity, and the modern love of the mirror — the endless beholding and adorning of the natural face, the culture that bids a man look within and admire what he finds — is the same haughtiness Isaiah names. The LORD threatens to take away the glasses with all the finery, for the self that gazes on itself will not gaze on God. To make the looking-glass a throne is to worship the creature and forget the Judge who sees the heart.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the plain object, but the principle to recover is which mirror we consult. The glass of self flatters and forgets; the glass of the Word shows a man his true face and calls him to be a doer, not a forgetful hearer (Jas 1:23). Best of all is the glass of Christ’s glory, in which the believer beholds not himself but his Lord, and beholding is changed into the same image, from glory to glory. Turn from the mirror that admires the flesh to the mirror that conforms the soul.
roots_summary: The word means a mirror of polished metal, giving a dim reflected image.
roots_lines: Glass — Old English glæs, here a mirror, not a pane.
Anciently a disc of polished metal for beholding the face.
In Isaiah, the hand-mirrors among the finery of Zion’s daughters.
It figures partial knowledge, seen “through a glass, darkly.”
It figures the Word and the glory of Christ, wherein we are changed.
usage: The glasses of Zion’s daughters were the tools of vanity, swept away in the day of judgment.
Now we see through a glass, darkly; then, face to face — our knowledge grows to sight.

etymology: An older variant of example, from Old French essample, itself from the Latin exemplum, “a sample, a pattern, that which is taken out and set forth for imitation.”
biblical_def: An ensample is an example, a pattern set forth for imitation or for warning — that which is taken out and held up that others may copy it or be admonished by it. The word carries a solemn weight in the epistles. Of Israel’s tempting and murmuring in the wilderness Paul writes, “Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come” (1Co 10:11). The judgments recorded in the Old Testament are not dead history but living warnings, God’s pattern-book for the church. The apostles themselves stood as ensamples: Paul bids the Thessalonians follow him, and commends them that they in turn “were ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia” (1Th 1:7), and elsewhere labours with his own hands to make himself “an ensample unto you to follow us” (2Th 3:9). Chiefly the word governs the ministry: Peter charges the elders to feed the flock “neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3). Here is the pastoral doctrine plainly — the shepherd rules not by lordly compulsion but by pattern, going before the sheep in the very holiness he preaches. A life is the sermon that cannot be gainsaid. The ensample of Israel warns; the ensample of the apostle draws; and above both stands Christ, who left us an ensample that we should follow His steps.
webster_summary: An example; a pattern set forth for imitation or for warning.
webster_full: ENSAMPLE, an old form of example; a pattern; a model for imitation.
That which is taken out and set forth that others may copy it.
Israel’s judgments are ensamples written for our admonition (1Co 10:11).
The apostles made themselves ensamples for the churches to follow.
Elders are to be ensamples to the flock, not lords over it (1Pe 5:3).
scriptures: Now all these things happened unto them for ensamples: and they are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come.
So that ye were ensamples to all that believe in Macedonia and Achaia.
Not because we have not power, but to make ourselves an ensample unto you to follow us.

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for a pattern; it recovers that Scripture’s history is written for our warning and that leaders rule by example.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that reads the Old Testament as dead history and its own leaders as mere managers. Paul says the murmurings and idolatries of the wilderness “happened unto them for ensamples” and were written for our admonition — a warning-book for the church, that we lust not, nor tempt Christ, nor murmur as they did. To dismiss those judgments as ancient and irrelevant is to despise the very instruction God set before us upon whom the ends of the world are come.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is government by pattern rather than by lordship. Peter forbids the elder to be a lord over God’s heritage and commands him to be an ensample to the flock — to go before the sheep in the holiness he preaches, so that his life is a sermon none can gainsay. A minister who commands what he will not do teaches the flock to despise the command; but the shepherd who is himself an ensample draws the sheep after Christ, whose steps he follows.
roots_summary: The word means an example, a pattern set forth for imitation or warning.
roots_lines: Ensample — an older variant of example.
From Old French essample, from Latin exemplum, “a sample, pattern.”

Israel’s history stands as an ensample of warning to the church.
The apostle and the elder stand as ensamples of imitation to the flock.
usage: All these things happened for ensamples: the wilderness is God’s warning-book for the church.
The Thessalonians became ensamples to all that believe, a pattern of faith spread abroad.

etymology: From the Latin penuria, “want, scarcity, dearth,” through Old French; hence extreme poverty, indigence, the utter lack of the means of living.
biblical_def: Penury is want in its severest degree — not merely a lean purse but destitution, the pinch of having next to nothing. Solomon sets it against the fruit of honest work: “In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23). The diligent hand comes to increase, but the mouth full of empty words comes to want; idle talk feeds no household, and the sluggard’s poverty is the wage of his tongue. Yet Scripture’s highest use of the word turns poverty into glory. Watching the treasury, our Lord saw the rich cast in of their abundance, and a poor widow cast in two mites; and He said, “of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had” (Luk 21:4). She gave not out of surplus but out of destitution — not what she could spare but all that she had, her whole living. The measure of the gift in heaven’s account is not the sum in the box but the love and faith in the hand that dropped it. The widow of penury outgave the wealthy, for she kept back nothing and trusted God for her next loaf. So the word rebukes both the idle tongue that talks itself into want and the full purse that gives only its leavings, and it exalts the poor saint whose empty hand is rich toward God.
webster_summary: Extreme poverty; want; destitution of the means of living.
webster_full: PENURY, want of the means of living; extreme poverty; indigence.
It is not a lean purse only but destitution, the pinch of having nothing.
The end of idle talk, as diligent labour is the way to profit (Pro 14:23).
Out of her penury the widow cast in all her living (Luk 21:4).
Heaven measures the gift not by the sum but by what is kept back.
scriptures: In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
Luk 21:4
For all these have of their abundance cast in unto the offerings of God: but she of her penury hath cast in all the living that she had.
Pro 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
How that in a great trial of affliction the abundance of their joy and their deep poverty abounded unto the riches of their liberality.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for destitution; it recovers the profit of labour and the widow whose empty hand outgave the rich.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age of many words and little work. Solomon says the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury: the tongue that promises and boasts and debates, while the hand lies idle, talks a man straight into want. Diligent labour has profit in it, but empty speech feeds no household. There is a warning here against the mouth that is always full and the hand that is always empty — against mistaking talk for toil, and the appearance of industry for its substance.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the arithmetic of heaven, which reckons a gift not by what is given but by what is kept back. The rich cast in of their abundance and were not the poorer for it; the widow cast in of her penury — two mites, but all her living — and gave more than they all. To give out of destitution and trust God for the next loaf is faith made visible. The empty hand that keeps back nothing is rich toward God, and the LORD who saw the widow’s mites has not forgotten them.
roots_summary: The word means extreme poverty, the want of the means of living.
roots_lines: Penury — from Latin penuria, “want, scarcity, dearth.”
It denotes destitution, poverty in its severest degree.
It is the end of idle talk, against the profit of labour (Pro 14:23).
Out of her penury the widow cast in all her living (Luk 21:4).
Heaven measures the gift by what is kept back, not by the sum.
usage: The talk of the lips tendeth to penury: many words and no work leave the household bare.
The widow of her penury cast in all her living, and outgave the rich in heaven’s account.
Deep poverty abounded unto liberality: penury is no bar to a generous, believing heart.

etymology: From the Old English lēasung, “lying, falsehood,” from lēas, “false, empty, void”; hence a lie, deception, the speaking of that which is not true. It has no kinship with the modern “lease” of property.
biblical_def: Leasing is the old Saxon word for lying — not the letting of land, but falsehood, the deliberate speaking of what is empty and untrue. The KJV keeps it in two psalms of David, where it names a sin the LORD abhors. “O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame? how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing?” (Psa 4:2). To love vanity and seek after leasing is to set the affection on emptiness and pursue the lie — to prefer the flattering falsehood to the weighty truth of God. David couples the love of vanity with the seeking of leasing, for the two go together: the heart that treasures empty things will gladly speak and believe empty words. In the fifth psalm the sin meets its judgment: “Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man” (Psa 5:6). The God of truth cannot look upon the lie; the liar and the murderer are named in one breath as objects of His abhorrence, for both destroy — the one the body, the other the truth. Against all leasing stands Christ, who is the Truth, in whose mouth was no guile, and the new man is bidden put away lying and speak every man truth with his neighbour. The tongue that seeks after leasing courts the abhorrence of God; the tongue that loves truth is conformed to the God of truth.
webster_summary: Lying; falsehood; the speaking of that which is untrue — not the letting of property.
webster_full: LEASING, falsehood; lies; the act or habit of lying.
From the Saxon lēas, “false, empty, void”; wholly distinct from the “lease” of land.
To seek after leasing is to pursue the lie and love vanity (Psa 4:2).
The LORD will destroy them that speak leasing (Psa 5:6).
The liar is named with the murderer as abhorred of a God of truth.
scriptures: Psa 4:2
O ye sons of men, how long will ye turn my glory into shame? how long will ye love vanity, and seek after leasing? Selah.
Psa 5:6
Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.
Lying lips are abomination to the LORD: but they that deal truly are his delight.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
corruption_summary: A word the age still needs, for leasing is lying, and no generation has loved the flattering falsehood more than ours.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a live corruption, and it is named plainly in Scripture’s vocabulary: leasing is the lie, and the age loves it. David asks how long men will love vanity and seek after leasing — and the question rebukes a generation that has learned to call the lie by softer names, to prize the flattering falsehood above the weighty truth, and to turn God’s glory into shame. The heart that loves emptiness will speak emptiness; the culture that treasures vanity will seek after leasing, believing the smooth thing and hating the reprover at the gate.

The judgment is not hidden. “Thou shalt destroy them that speak leasing: the LORD will abhor the bloody and deceitful man.” The God of truth names the liar with the murderer, for both are destroyers — the one of the body, the other of the truth by which souls live. And the Revelation shuts all liars out of the city, giving them their part in the lake of fire. Against every leasing stands Christ, in whose mouth was found no guile; the new man puts away lying and speaks truth, for he serves a God who cannot lie.
roots_summary: The word means lying, falsehood — the speaking of what is empty and untrue.
roots_lines: Leasing — Old English lēasung, “lying, falsehood.”
From lēas, “false, empty, void”; no kin to the modern “lease.”

The liar is abhorred with the murderer by the God of truth.
usage: Leasing is not the letting of land but the lie: to seek after leasing is to court God’s abhorrence.
How long will ye love vanity and seek after leasing? The empty heart speaks empty words.
The LORD destroys them that speak leasing, naming the liar with the murderer as a destroyer.

etymology: From the Latin victualia, “provisions,” from victus, “food, sustenance, that by which one lives” (from vivere, “to live”), through Old French; hence food, provisions, the stores that sustain life. Commonly in the plural, victuals.
biblical_def: Victual is food — provisions, the stores of bread and meat by which life is sustained. The word marks the Exodus at its haste: Israel “baked unleavened cakes of the dough which they brought forth out of Egypt… because they were thrust out… and could not tarry, neither had they prepared for themselves any victual” (Exo 12:39). Redemption came so suddenly there was no time to leaven the bread or pack a provision; they went out trusting the God who would rain manna. In settled days victual is the labour of stewards: Solomon set twelve officers over Israel who “provided victuals for the king and his household” (1Ki 4:7), a picture of ordered plenty under a peaceable reign. Nehemiah’s people covenant not to buy victuals of the heathen on the sabbath (Neh 10:31), guarding the holy day from the traffic of the market. And in the gospel the word turns to a miracle: at evening in the desert the disciples urged, “send the multitude away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves victuals” (Mat 14:15) — but Christ would not send them away hungry. He took five loaves and fed five thousand, that they need buy no victual, for the Bread of life was in their midst. So the word runs from the unleavened haste of the Exodus to the overflowing baskets of Galilee, and everywhere it preaches the same lesson: man lives not by bread alone, but by the God who provides the bread.
webster_summary: Food; provisions; the stores of meat and bread by which life is sustained.
webster_full: VICTUAL, food; provisions; stores for the sustenance of life. Chiefly in the plural, victuals.
From the Latin victus, “that by which one lives.”
Israel left Egypt in haste, with no victual prepared (Exo 12:39).
Solomon’s officers provided victuals for the king and his household (1Ki 4:7).
In the desert Christ fed the multitude that need buy no victuals (Mat 14:15).

And Solomon had twelve officers over all Israel, which provided victuals for the king and his household: each man his month in a year made provision.

And if the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the sabbath, or on the holy day: and that we would leave the seventh year, and the exaction of every debt.
And when it was evening, his disciples came to him, saying, This is a desert place, and the time is now past; send the multitude away, that they may go into the villages, and buy themselves victuals.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a plain word for food; it recovers that our daily victual is the gift of a providing God.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a heart anxious for provision and forgetful of the Provider. Israel left Egypt with no victual prepared, thrust out in haste, and the God who redeemed them rained bread from heaven forty years. Nehemiah’s people would not so much as buy their victuals on the sabbath, holding the day of God above the traffic of the market — a reproof to an age that treats no hour as holy and no bread as a gift. To trust God for the next meal, and to keep His day even when the market calls, is faith in the God who feeds His own.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that man lives not by bread alone. When the disciples would send the multitude away to buy victuals, Christ took five loaves and fed five thousand, that they need buy nothing, for the Bread of life was among them. The daily victual points beyond itself: he who has Christ has the true food that endureth unto everlasting life. Give us this day our daily bread is a prayer to the Father who clothes the lilies and feeds the ravens, and who will not send His children away hungry.
roots_summary: The word means food, provisions, the stores by which life is sustained.

etymology: From the Greek nitron and Hebrew nether, a natural mineral alkali (native soda or carbonate of soda), used anciently as a cleansing agent and effervescing sharply when met with an acid like vinegar.
biblical_def: Nitre in the KJV is not our gunpowder saltpetre but the ancient washing-soda, a natural alkali dug from the earth and used as soap to scour and cleanse. Solomon employs its chemistry for a proverb of the heart: “As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart” (Pro 25:20). Vinegar poured on nitre hisses and boils and is spoiled, and the two war against each other; so mirth forced upon a grieving soul does not soothe but frets, the wrong remedy at the wrong hour. The word’s deeper use is in Jeremiah, where the LORD confronts a nation that would scrub away its guilt: “For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord GOD” (Jer 2:22). Here is the whole doctrine of sin and self-salvation. Nitre and soap will cleanse the garment and the flesh, but no alkali of earth reaches the stain of iniquity. Let a man wash with all the nitre of his good works, his penances, his reformations, and take never so much soap of ceremony, and the mark of his sin stands out the plainer before God. There is but one laver that avails: “the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin.” The nitre of works cannot whiten what only the blood of Christ can wash white as snow.
webster_summary: An ancient mineral alkali or washing-soda used as soap; in Jeremiah, a figure of the works that cannot cleanse sin.
webster_full: NITRE, a native mineral alkali, the washing-soda of the ancients, used to scour and cleanse.
It is not the saltpetre of later use, but a carbonate of soda.
Poured on with vinegar it effervesces and is spoiled (Pro 25:20).
As soap it cleanses the garment, but not the stain of iniquity (Jer 2:22).
It figures the works of self-cleansing that cannot reach the guilt of sin.

Jer 2:22
For though thou wash thee with nitre, and take thee much soap, yet thine iniquity is marked before me, saith the Lord GOD.
Psa 51:2

corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but an old cleansing salt; it recovers the truth that no soap of works can wash away sin, but only the blood of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the ancient and ever-living error of self-cleansing. Jeremiah’s people thought to scour their guilt with nitre and much soap — with reformation, ceremony, and the labour of their own hands — and the LORD answered that their iniquity was marked before Him still. The age is full of such washing: the man who would scrub his conscience clean by good deeds, by making amends, by turning over a new leaf, and who finds the stain the plainer for his scrubbing. No alkali of earth reaches the deep dye of sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that there is one laver only. David did not cry, Give me nitre and soap, but “Wash me throughly from mine iniquity” — a washing that God alone can give. The blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanseth us from all sin, and it alone. Let a man wash with all the nitre of his works and take never so much soap of religion; the mark remains until the blood of Christ washes him white as snow. Salvation is not scoured out by the sinner but poured in by the Saviour.
roots_summary: The word means an ancient mineral alkali or washing-soda used to cleanse.

As soap it cleanses the garment but not the stain of sin (Jer 2:22).
It figures the works of self-cleansing that cannot reach iniquity.
usage: As vinegar upon nitre, so are forced songs to a heavy heart — the wrong balm hisses and frets.
Though thou wash with nitre and much soap, thine iniquity is marked before God still.
No nitre of works whitens the soul; only the blood of Christ cleanseth from all sin.

etymology: From the Old French lachet, a diminutive of laz (“a lace, a snare”), from the Latin laqueus, “a noose, a cord”; hence the thong or lace that binds a sandal to the foot.
biblical_def: A latchet is the leather thong or lace that fastens a sandal to the foot — the smallest, meanest strap of a man’s apparel, and the very sign of a menial errand, for to unloose it was the office of the lowest slave. Abram, refusing the spoils of Sodom’s king, swears he will not take “from a thread even to a shoelatchet” (Gen 14:23) — not the least and cheapest thing — lest a heathen king should say he had made Abram rich; the patriarch would owe his wealth to God alone. Isaiah, describing the ready and unwearied army the LORD summons, says “neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken” (Isa 5:27): their equipment is perfect, not a strap gives way. But the word’s glory is on the lips of John the Baptist. Pointing away from himself to the Coming One, he says of Christ, “the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose” (Mar 1:7), and again, “whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose” (Luk 3:16). The greatest born of women counts himself unfit for the slave’s lowest task before the Lord — not worthy even to touch the latchet of His sandal. Here is the measure of Christ’s greatness and the pattern of all true humility: the nearer a man comes to the majesty of the Son of God, the lower he stoops, until the loftiest saint is glad to be found at His feet, unfit even to loose the latchet.
webster_summary: The thong or lace that fastens a sandal to the foot; the meanest strap, whose unloosing was a slave’s office.
webster_full: LATCHET, the string or thong that fastens a shoe or sandal.
From the Latin laqueus, “a noose or cord.”
The least and cheapest part of apparel, as “a thread… to a shoelatchet” (Gen 14:23).
To unloose it was the office of the lowest servant.
John counted himself unworthy to loose the latchet of Christ’s shoes (Mar 1:7).
scriptures: That I will not take from a thread even to a shoelatchet, and that I will not take any thing that is thine, lest thou shouldest say, I have made Abram rich:
Isa 5:27
None shall be weary nor stumble among them; none shall slumber nor sleep; neither shall the girdle of their loins be loosed, nor the latchet of their shoes be broken:
Mar 1:7
And preached, saying, There cometh one mightier than I after me, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and unloose.
Luk 3:16

John answered, saying unto them all, I indeed baptize you with water; but one mightier than I cometh, the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to unloose: he shall baptize you with the Holy Ghost and with fire:
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the humble word for a sandal-string; it recovers the greatness of Christ and the lowliness of true humility.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes the pride of an age that will stoop to no one. Abram would not take so much as a shoelatchet from the king of Sodom, refusing to owe the least thing to a heathen hand, that God alone might have the glory of his riches — a rebuke to every soul that grasps at gain from tainted sources. And the latchet, the meanest strap of the foot, marks the lowest service, the task the proud disdain. The man who counts no work beneath him has learned a lesson the world despises.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is measured by the sandal-thong. John the Baptist, than whom none greater was born of women, judged himself unworthy to stoop and unloose the latchet of Christ’s shoes — unfit for the slave’s lowest office before his Lord. Here is the greatness of Christ, before whom the loftiest saint is small, and the pattern of humility: the nearer we draw to His majesty, the lower we bow. To think ourselves unworthy even to touch His latchet is not false modesty but the sober truth of a creature before his God.
roots_summary: The word means the thong or lace that fastens a sandal to the foot.
roots_lines: Latchet — Old French lachet, from Latin laqueus, “a cord, a noose.”
It denotes the leather thong that binds the sandal to the foot.
The least and cheapest part of apparel, from thread to shoelatchet (Gen 14:23).
To unloose it was the office of the lowest slave.
John was unworthy to loose the latchet of Christ’s shoes (Mar 1:7).
usage: Abram would not take a shoelatchet of Sodom, that God alone should have his riches.
Not a latchet broken among them: the LORD’s summoned host is armed and unwearied.
John was unworthy to unloose the latchet of Christ’s shoe — the measure of the Saviour’s greatness.

etymology: From self + edge, literally the “self-edge” — the woven border of a cloth finished so that it will not ravel or unravel; a self-finished margin. A KJV hapax, occurring but once.
biblical_def: A selvedge is the self-finished edge of a woven cloth — the border woven back upon itself so that the fabric will not fray or unravel at the margin. It occurs but once in all Scripture, in the making of the tabernacle’s inner curtains: “thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second” (Exo 26:4). The ten linen curtains of the sanctuary were not left as ten separate cloths but joined: at the selvedge, the finished outer border, loops of blue were set, and by golden taches the curtains were coupled “together one to another” (Exo 26:3), that “it shall be one tabernacle.” The doctrine is woven into the very edge. The dwelling-place of God is not a heap of loose pieces but a fabric knit into one — every curtain bound to its fellow along a strong, unfraying border. So the church is many members compacted into one body: “the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth” (Eph 4:16), knit into one by the golden taches of the Spirit and the bond of love. The selvedge preaches that God’s house holds together at the edges — that the saints are not a scattering of solitary threads but a woven unity, each joined to each, and the whole made one habitation of God through the Spirit.
webster_summary: The self-finished woven border of a cloth that keeps it from raveling; in Exodus, the edge where the tabernacle curtains were coupled into one.
webster_full: SELVEDGE, the edge of cloth so woven that it will not ravel; the self-finished border.
Literally the “self-edge,” from self and edge.
It occurs but once in Scripture, a KJV hapax (Exo 26:4).
At the selvedge the loops of blue were set to couple the curtains.
By it the ten curtains were joined into one tabernacle.
scriptures: Exo 26:4

And thou shalt make loops of blue upon the edge of the one curtain from the selvedge in the coupling; and likewise shalt thou make in the uttermost edge of another curtain, in the coupling of the second.
Exo 26:3
The five curtains shall be coupled together one to another; and other five curtains shall be coupled one to another.
Exo 26:6
And thou shalt make fifty taches of gold, and couple the curtains together with the taches: and it shall be one tabernacle.
Eph 4:16

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but a weaver’s finished edge; it recovers the unity of God’s house, knit together at the selvedge into one.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes an age that prizes the solitary thread and despises the joining. The selvedge is the edge that will not ravel, the border by which one curtain is coupled to its fellow; and God ordered His dwelling to be no loose collection of cloths but a woven unity. The modern temper, which exalts the independent self and holds membership in a body to be optional, would leave the curtains unjoined — but a curtain without its selvedge frays, and a saint without the fellowship of the saints unravels at the edge. God’s house is built by coupling, not by scattering.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the knit unity of the church. The ten curtains, joined at the selvedge by loops of blue and taches of gold, became one tabernacle; and the whole body, fitly joined together and compacted, maketh increase unto the edifying of itself in love. Every member is bound to his fellow along a strong, unfraying border, and the whole is made one habitation of God through the Spirit. Let no saint think himself a solitary thread: he is woven into the fabric, joined at the edge, and the dwelling-place of God holds together in the coupling.
roots_summary: The word means the self-finished woven border of a cloth that keeps it from raveling.
roots_lines: Selvedge — from self + edge, the “self-edge.”
It is the woven border finished so the cloth will not ravel.
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (Exo 26:4).
At the selvedge the loops of blue coupled the curtains together.
It figures the church, knit into one body at the edges (Eph 4:16).
usage: The loops of blue were set from the selvedge, that curtain might couple to curtain.
A cloth without its selvedge frays; a saint apart from the body unravels at the edge.
The selvedge preaches unity: God’s house is woven into one, joined member to member.

etymology: From the Latin malefactor, “an evil-doer,” from male (“evilly, ill”) and facere (“to do”); hence one who does evil, a criminal, a doer of wickedness worthy of punishment.
biblical_def: A malefactor is an evil-doer — one who does ill, a criminal condemned for his crimes. The word belongs almost wholly to the passion of our Lord, where it is heavy with a terrible irony. Two malefactors were led out with Jesus to be put to death (Luk 23:32), and at Calvary “they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left” (Luk 23:33). The sinless Son of God was numbered with transgressors, hung between two criminals as though He were the chief of them — He who did no evil, crucified in the place of evil-doers, that He might bear their evil in His own body on the tree. One of the malefactors railed on Him (Luk 23:39), but the other, rebuking his fellow and owning his own just condemnation, turned to Christ with the dying prayer, “Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom” — and heard the word of paradise. Here is sovereign grace at its plainest: a malefactor, nailed fast in his last hour, with no work to offer and no time to mend, saved by a look to Christ. The word’s bitterest use is on the lips of Christ’s accusers, who told Pilate, “If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee” (Joh 18:30) — the world calling the one sinless Man a malefactor, condemning Righteousness itself. So the guilty thief was justified and the guiltless Saviour condemned, that evil-doers might be made righteous through the blood of the Innocent.
webster_summary: An evil-doer; a criminal; one guilty of crime and worthy of punishment.
webster_full: MALEFACTOR, one who does evil; a criminal; an offender against law.
From the Latin male, “ill,” and facere, “to do.”
Two malefactors were crucified with Christ (Luk 23:33).
One railed on Him; the other believed and heard the word of paradise (Luk 23:39).
The accusers called the sinless Christ a malefactor (Joh 18:30).
scriptures: And there were also two other, malefactors, led with him to be put to death.
And when they were come to the place, which is called Calvary, there they crucified him, and the malefactors, one on the right hand, and the other on the left.
And one of the malefactors which were hanged railed on him, saying, If thou be Christ, save thyself and us.
They answered and said unto him, If he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up unto thee.
corruption_summary: Not a contested doctrine but the plain word for an evil-doer; it recovers the sinless Christ numbered with transgressors and the malefactor saved by grace alone.
corruption_paragraphs: The word rebukes a world that calls good evil and evil good. Christ’s accusers stood before Pilate and named the one sinless Man a malefactor — “if he were not a malefactor, we would not have delivered him up” — condemning Righteousness itself and preferring Barabbas the murderer. So the age still arraigns Christ and His holiness as the wrongdoer, and honours the transgressor. To see the Lord of glory numbered with the malefactors and crucified between them is to see the depth of human enmity against God, and the depth of His love, who was made sin for us though He knew no sin.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is grace to the guilty. One malefactor, nailed fast with no hour left to work and no deed to offer, owned his just condemnation, turned to Christ, and prayed to be remembered — and was told, “To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” Here is salvation stripped to its bones: not of works, lest any man should boast, but by a look of faith to the Saviour dying at his side. If a malefactor in his last breath may be received, then no sinner who comes to Christ shall be cast out; but let none presume, for one thief was saved and the other railed and perished.
roots_summary: The word means an evil-doer, a criminal guilty of crime.
roots_lines: Malefactor — Latin male, “ill,” and facere, “to do.”
It denotes one who does evil, a doer of wickedness.
Two malefactors were crucified with Christ at Calvary (Luk 23:33).
The penitent thief, a malefactor, was received into paradise.
The accusers called the sinless Christ a malefactor (Joh 18:30).
usage: Christ was numbered with malefactors, crucified between two, that He might bear their evil.
A dying malefactor, with no work to offer, was saved by a look to Christ — grace alone.
The world called the sinless Saviour a malefactor, condemning Righteousness itself.
